en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Mad Dog, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty.
The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha; it was the fifteenth day of the month, the time for the recitation of the precepts. At that time...
Ānanda knelt down with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Now the Buddha is the savior of all; you enlighten and transform those who are ignorant, blind, and deluded within the five realms of existence, causing them to escape the evil paths.”

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he leaves behind his relics and the twelve divisions of the scriptures in the world. You disciples should rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to transmit the Buddha’s scriptures and precepts, deliver sentient beings, and bestow the rules of discipline upon them, causing people to make offerings; this shall be no different from the presence of the Buddha himself.
The Buddha said:
"If there is someone who receives the precepts from one of my disciples, yet subsequently feels envy toward that teacher, this person must have come from the evil realms."
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
“What is meant by ‘unwholesome realms’?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In the time of a past Buddha, there was a rabid dog that bit its own master;

that previous Buddha, out of compassion, offered a prayer for the dog's sake. Upon seeing the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the dog immediately felt joy, yet this dog is now in the hells, its retribution for sin not yet exhausted."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his karmic retribution having been exhausted, he was reborn into the human realm because of his former joy; he received the precepts from my disciple, specifically from the one who was the master when [the dog] acted as a mad dog. Because the dog possessed residual consciousness, it returned to bite its own master.
The Buddha said:

“If there is someone who receives the precepts from a teacher and yet slanders that teacher, speaking ill of him and saying, ‘He does not practice what he teaches,’ such a person is like a rabid dog that turns back to bite its own master.
One who slanders the Teacher of the Way as being evil was originally a dog in a past life.”
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
“When the dog’s transgressions are exhausted and it enters the human realm, for what reason does it return again to bite its former master?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"This dog has entered the human path and upheld the Buddha’s precepts and Dharma; yet, having been taught and instructed, he became greedy for profit and offerings, and being foolish and ignorant, he proceeded to slander his teacher. For this reason, he has fallen into the evil realm of the five heinous crimes."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Listen attentively!
The Buddha shall explain it to you in full."
Ānanda said: “Yes! I accept your instruction.”
The Buddha said,
"There are those who uphold the Dharma and precepts of the Buddha, yet teach others to serve the Buddha while causing them to enter the niraya hells.
Ānanda rose in alarm, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and asked the Buddha:
"How can one teach others so that they may attain the Buddha-way, yet enter further into the hells?
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you believe my words?"
Ānanda said, "I believe the Buddha's words.
The Buddha said:
"If you believe the Buddha's words, why are you startled upon hearing that a person who has received the precepts will enter niraya?
If such a person does not enter niraya, would the Buddha's words then be false?"
Ānanda rose again, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, circumambulated the Buddha three times, returned to take hold of the Buddha’s feet, knelt for a long time, and asked the Buddha:
“I, Ānanda, do not understand; I do not yet know the faculties of people.”
"I pray that the Buddha will explain this and teach people how to enter the state of mind that leads to the hells.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In the future, at the end of the age, there will be disciples who act as teachers; they will be indolent and unable to study diligently, possessing no wisdom."
They are defiled by greed, desiring to receive offerings of money, grain, and silk from others to sustain themselves;

they do not apply themselves diligently to the Buddha-dharma, but instead flatter and follow the whims of others; seeing people who are greedy for killing, they do not bestow the precept against killing upon them;
seeing people who crave wine, they do not forbid it, claiming that small amounts may be drunk.
When one person bestows the dharma of precepts upon another, they say that by giving a certain amount of money or goods, one shall gain merit;
yet this is merely a desire to obtain the property of others, which constitutes selling the precepts and making a person into a slave.
Furthermore, those who harbor arrogance and are not diligent regarding the precepts commit the grave offense of killing sentient beings.
One who teaches in such a manner causes people to fall into the hells (*niraya*).

Because they have violated the Buddha’s clear teachings, the deities who protect the Buddha’s Way will find their weakness; they will then be afflicted by evil spirits, suffering so severely that it may even lead to death. Having paid for their transgressions, they shall enter the hells.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
“Those who have newly resolved their minds may happen to encounter an evil teacher;
not understanding clearly, they claim that such is the nature of the Dharma, leading them to believe and accept his words because of their ignorance and lack of comprehension.”
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"If one encounters another enlightened teacher, may one receive the precepts again?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Within my Dharma, there is vastness and magnanimity; one can certainly repent and wash away their transgressions.
When you first resolved to attain enlightenment, your mind was constantly clouded and obscured, and you were misled by evil teachers, truly not knowing for yourself;
only by receiving the precepts once more have you begun to enter the Dharma."
"When one does not know and does not understand, one is not a disciple of the Buddha; such a person is merely a minor virtuous individual of the world and possesses no great merit.
Having heard what the Buddha said, Ānanda rejoiced and paid homage.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Mad Dog.
